passage:
Alka: hey sorry!! can't come for the film tomorrow 😣 Ma says I have to go to my cousin's engagement
Bhupen: fine, whatever
(Bhupen tossed his phone onto the bed and went back to his maths homework. He'd been looking forward to the film all week and had already checked the show timings. A bit of a letdown, that was all. He'd ask her about next Sunday after dinner.)
Alka: ...
Alka: ok
Alka: are you mad at me??
Alka: I literally can't skip it, it's family
(The messages sat unread. Bhupen's phone lay face down under a pillow, buzzing softly while he fought with a quadratic equation.)
Alka: bhupen??
Alka: ok forget it

qa.q: Why couldn't Alka come for the film?
qa.a: Ma said she had to go to her cousin's engagement.

qa.q: What did Bhupen actually feel when he typed 'fine, whatever'?
qa.a: Only mild disappointment; he'd been looking forward to the film but planned to ask about next Sunday.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do now to stop the misunderstanding from growing?
qa.a: Check his phone and add a friendly line, like 'Not mad, just bummed. Next Sunday?', so Alka hears the tone his two words left out.

qa.q: How is Alka reading 'fine, whatever' and the silence after it?
qa.a: Without his voice or face, she reads the short words as anger, and the unread messages make her more anxious 😰.

grounding: A teenage boy sends 'fine, whatever' after a friend cancels, meaning mild disappointment, while the bare words read as anger.

passage: The power had gone out again in Saoner, and Jatin was sitting on the rooftop with his phone at eleven per cent. Ramesh's message came in: 'Bro can't come to the dam tomorrow. Papa needs me at the shop, sorry.' Jatin sighed. He'd fixed the chain on his cycle specially. He typed 'fine, whatever' and sent it, then switched the phone off to save the battery. In his head it was just a shrug, the way he'd say it with a half-smile if Ramesh were standing in front of him. Across town, Ramesh stared at the two words under the shop's flickering tube light. No emoji. No 'next time'. Just 'whatever'. He read it three times, and each time it sounded angrier.

qa.q: What had Jatin fixed specially for the trip?
qa.a: He'd fixed the chain on his cycle specially.

qa.q: What did Jatin mean by 'fine, whatever'?
qa.a: It was just a shrug of mild disappointment, the kind he'd say with a half-smile in person, not anger.

qa.q: What small change could have kept Jatin's message from being misread?
qa.a: Adding a friendly word or 'next time?' before switching off his phone would have carried the half-smile that the bare words lost.

qa.q: What is Ramesh experiencing as he rereads the two words?
qa.a: Without Jatin's voice or face, the message sounds angrier each time, and Ramesh likely feels guilty and worried that his friend is upset.

grounding: A small-town teen sends 'fine, whatever' meaning only a shrug, and without his voice or face his friend reads it as anger.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, Saturday
Jyoti was sitting in the common room after lunch, ready to go out, when her friend Mitali messaged to cancel their plan to see the craft fair. Jyoti read it, sighed, and typed "fine, whatever", then put her phone face down and picked up a magazine. She did not seem angry to me. A little flat, maybe disappointed, but she was chatting with the younger girls a minute later.
When I asked about it, she said, "It's no big deal. I just wanted to go."
I told her that without her face or voice, "fine, whatever" can look quite cross on a screen. She looked surprised and picked up her phone again.
Deepika, warden

qa.q: What did Jyoti type after Mitali cancelled?
qa.a: "fine, whatever"

qa.q: What was Jyoti actually feeling when she typed the message?
qa.a: She felt mildly disappointed and a bit flat, not angry, since she soon chatted with the younger girls.

qa.q: What small step could Jyoti take next, now that she has picked up her phone?
qa.a: Add a short clear line, such as "just a bit sad, next weekend?", so Mitali doesn't read anger into it.

qa.q: How might Mitali read "fine, whatever" on her screen?
qa.a: Without Jyoti's face or voice, Mitali may read it as angry and feel guilty or worried.

grounding: Shows a teen sending "fine, whatever" after a cancelled plan, meaning only mild disappointment that could read as anger.

passage:
Diary, Sunday
Jeevan cancelled the cycle ride this morning. Again. Well, only the second time. He said his cousins had come over.
I was already in my shoes. I typed "fine, whatever" and went back to bed. I wasn't mad, really. Just a bit let down. I'd pumped the tyres last night and everything.
Now it's evening and he hasn't replied. Not even a thumbs-up. Which is weird for him.
I scrolled up and read my message again, like he would. "fine, whatever." Hmm. On its own, it looks pretty angry, doesn't it? In my head it sounded like a shrug.
Nikita

qa.q: What had Nikita done to the tyres the night before?
qa.a: Pumped the tyres.

qa.q: What was Nikita actually feeling when sending "fine, whatever"?
qa.a: Nikita felt a bit let down and disappointed, not angry, meaning the message as a shrug.

qa.q: What could Nikita do now that the message looks angry on rereading?
qa.a: Send a quick follow-up like "not mad, just sad we missed it, next week?" to add the missing tone.

qa.q: What might Jeevan be feeling in his silence?
qa.a: Jeevan may be reading the message as anger and feel guilty or hurt, unsure how to reply.

grounding: Shows a teen realising that "fine, whatever", meant as mild disappointment, can read as anger without tone or face.

passage: Mridul had cleaned both bicycles that morning. The plan was to ride to the temple fair outside Barsana after lunch, buy jalebi and try the ring-toss again. At twelve his phone buzzed: "sorry bhai cant come, mamaji visiting, mummy says stay home". Mridul sat on the verandah step, looking at the two shining bikes. He felt a small dip in his chest; nothing big, just flat. He typed "fine, whatever", pressed send, and went to help his father unload rice sacks from the tractor. What he meant was: okay, a bit sad, next time. He didn't think about how the words would look on a small screen, with no face and no voice behind them, arriving at Pranav's house just as the guests were being served tea.

qa.q: What did Mridul type after Pranav cancelled?
qa.a: He typed "fine, whatever" and pressed send.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when he sent the message?
qa.a: He felt mildly disappointed and flat, not angry; he meant okay, a bit sad, next time.

qa.q: What could Mridul have added to make the message clearer?
qa.a: A few words like "no problem, sad though, next week?" would show mild disappointment instead of sounding angry.

qa.q: How might Pranav read "fine, whatever" in the middle of serving guests?
qa.a: With no face or voice behind it, Pranav might take it as anger and feel guilty or stung.

grounding: Shows a teenager sending a short reply after a friend cancels, meaning mild disappointment, in words that can easily read as anger.
